### 7.2.1 Cognitive Architecture Under the Control of Algorithmic Latent Space

To understand how artificial intelligence-driven behavioral engineering threatens mental autonomy, we must first dismantle the myth that the human mind is an impenetrable fortress (Weizenbaum, 1976). In the modern digital landscape, our consciousness continuously interacts with interfaces neuro-psychologically engineered to bypass reflective thought processes (System 2, according to Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's dual-process cognitive taxonomy, 1974; Kahneman, 2011) and directly exploit intuitive, fast, and emotional thinking systems (System 1). GenAI algorithms and recommendation systems act as shadow architects that reconstruct the user's subjective reality, not through physical coercion, but through the curation of highly manipulative informational environments (Floridi, 2013).

Imagine this process as a painter secretly altering the pigment colors on the canvas of your world every second, until you come to believe that the sky is indeed pitch black and that the only way to save yourself is to purchase a product or embrace a specific narrative (Dreyfus, 1972). Within the digital sphere, the latent space of artificial intelligence models maps millions of psychographic parameters—ranging from levels of neuroticism and vulnerability to social anxiety, to political confirmation biases (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). When these systems generate text responses, video recommendations, or notifications micro-tailored to these profiles, they are not presenting objective information; they are triggering electrochemical responses within the brain designed to induce behavioral addiction (Farahany, 2023).

Empirical studies from various cyber-psychology research institutions indicate that continuous exposure to content feeds optimized for engagement metrics progressively weakens the capacity for executive function within the prefrontal cortex (Bowlby, 1969; Zuboff, 2019). Individuals lose the capacity for delayed gratification, experience a diminished attention span, and, most dangerously, undergo what we term the *outsourcing of agency*—a condition in which a person voluntarily surrenders life decisions, ranging from romantic affairs to political choices, to the pseudo-legitimacy conferred by chatbots or recommendation systems (Searle, 1980; Wiener, 1950). It is precisely here that mental autonomy undergoes a silent collapse; a will that appears autonomous on the surface is actually the end product of a chain of algorithmic manipulation operating entirely below the threshold of the legal subject's conscious awareness.
